extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and readers of fairy tales, fantasy, and imaginative literature; general literary readers seeking principles of wonder and storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and aesthetic criteria for creating/assessing fairy-tale and wonder-filled storytelling: how to evoke astonishment, set conditional magic, use limits and inventory, and ground criticism in loyalty rather than cynical detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fairy-tale language to express distinctness and wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: "This fairy-tale language about things is simply rational and agnostic. It is the only way I can express in words my clear and definite perception that one thing is quite distinct from another; that there is no logical connection between flying and laying eggs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write as if things are startlingly particular and not logically linked; present ordinary facts as discrete surprises. Anti-pattern: the scientific or sentimental habit of smudging separate phenomena into a supposed necessary 'law' (the professor who feels an illusory connection because he has often seen two things together). Use language that restores the perception of difference to renew astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch the instinct of astonishment (make the ordinary seem miraculous)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Astonishing tales ... touch the nerve of the ancient instinct of astonishment. ... A child of three is excited by being told that Tommy opened a door."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the immediate shock or surprise of events; often the smallest incident (opening a door) can yield wonder. For maximal effect, foreground the moment of discovery rather than elaborate explanation. Example: tales that make rivers run with wine remind us, for a moment, that rivers run with water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey gratitude and praise as a central emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The wonder has a positive element of praise. ... The test of all happiness is gratitude; and I felt grateful, though I hardly knew to whom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame characters' or narrator's reactions as gratefulness for existence or gifts rather than mere astonishment. Treat life and small gifts as presents (Chesterton's toy-legs/Santa Claus image). This emotional stance grounds wonder in praise rather than only curiosity or terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ the Doctrine of Conditional Joy (magic hinges on a veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the dizzy and colossal things conceded depend upon one small thing withheld. ... The vision always hangs upon a veto."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct magical or fantastical scenarios where extraordinary benefits depend on a specific prohibition or condition (the forbidden word, the thing not to be shown, the time limit). This single withheld thing provides dramatic tension and moral texture. Examples: 'do not say the word "cow"' or 'be back by twelve.' Anti-pattern: presenting boundless magic with no rule or cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect mysterious rules and lawfulness in fairyland
rubrics_metrics.description: "The true citizen of fairyland is obeying something that he does not understand at all. In the fairy tale an incomprehensible happiness rests upon an incomprehensible condition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the world internal rules that feel authoritative yet not fully explainable — obedience to such laws creates the ethical and emotional backbone of the tale. Avoid portraying fairyland as mere anarchic lawlessness; its power often comes from inscrutable commandments that characters must follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make happiness bright but brittle (fragility as a narrative quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This princess lives in a glass castle... this thin glitter of glass everywhere is the expression of the fact that the happiness is bright but brittle, like the substance most easily smashed by a housemaid or a cat."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagery and plot devices that emphasise the fragility of joy: shining, glass-like pleasures that can be lost by a small act. This heightens stakes and makes restraint meaningful. Also note: fragility is not identical with perishability — something breakable can endure if respected (don't strike the glass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a moral or symbolic price for extraordinary joy
rubrics_metrics.description: "The proper form of thanks to it is some form of humility and restraint: we should thank God for beer and Burgundy by not drinking too much of them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link aesthetic or miraculous rewards to acts of restraint, sacrifice, or obedience. Writers should show that great delight is paid for by symbolic acts (fasting, vows, keeping limits), rather than presented as cost-free abundance. Anti-pattern: aesthetes who feel intense joy but refuse any corresponding discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray repetition as willful choice (repetition as encore, not mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The repetition in Nature may not be a mere recurrence; it may be a theatrical ENCORE... It may be that God makes every daisy separately, but has never got tired of making them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using recurring patterns, treat them as deliberate, loving repetition rather than mechanical determinism. This gives repetition a poetic, celebratory tone (an 'encore') and preserves agency/meaning. Avoid rendering repetition as lifeless clockwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imply a personal purpose or storyteller behind the world
rubrics_metrics.description: "I had always felt life first as a story: and if there is a story there is a story-teller."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal that events arise from an intelligent will or artistic intention (a person behind the scene). This helps readers sense purpose and design in the narrative cosmos, strengthening the impression of mythic or theological significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate limits and scarcity to create value (poetry of limits / inventory)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Robinson Crusoe ... owes its eternal vivacity to the fact that it celebrates the poetry of limits ... The greatest of poems is an inventory. Every kitchen tool becomes ideal because Crusoe might have dropped it in the sea."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lists, inventories, and attention to salvaged or limited objects to make ordinary items resonate with meaning. Emphasise that scarcity and finitude make things precious. This technique turns domestic detail into romantic or sacred material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster primary loyalty/patriotism to the world rather than detached critique
rubrics_metrics.description: "My acceptance of the universe is not optimism, it is more like patriotism. ... He has a loyalty long before he has any admiration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing attitudes toward a place or world, write from a stance of committed love or allegiance rather than only evaluative distance. Show how attachment can inspire repair and decoration (loving Pimlico into beauty) and how devotion can be a creative force. Anti-pattern: the detached house-hunter attitude that treats the world as expendable lodging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cynical, malicious, or merely gloomy criticism (be candid from love, not hurt)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The evil of the pessimist is ... that he does not love what he chastises--he has not this primary and supernatural loyalty to things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique in fiction (or of the world within fiction) should come from a place of care and constructive motive; avoid using honesty as a cover for pleasure in tearing things down. Distinguish sincere advisers from the 'uncandid candid friend' who enjoys pessimism. This is both an ethical and aesthetic directive for tone and motive.
